mainTopic: Appraising damage to produce: what 'sixty' means, valuing crops by how they would grow, subtracting the owner's savings, and the final ruling on destroyed palms.
overview: The amud opens by finishing אביי's proof. A ברייתא about an animal that ate budding grapes has חכמים saying 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth,' and that wording must mean appraising against sixty, so the other ברייתא means sixty too. אביי then shows that רבי יוסי הגלילי and רבי ישמעאל agree: damage is valued by what is left in the field as it grows. רבי ישמעאל's 'מיטב' is not read like רב אידי בר אבין, because the one who wants to collect must bring proof. Next the גמרא resolves a contradiction inside the words of רבי שמעון בן יהודה, and רבינא joins the two parts into one statement. This makes him sound like רבי יהושע, so the גמרא says they differ about subtracting the 'weakening of the vine.' אביי proves that רבי שמעון בן יהודה is the one who subtracts it, from his ruling that a rapist does not pay for pain. אביי then links this to רבי יוסי and בן עזאי, who subtract the midwife cost or the extra food in a miscarriage case. Finally the גמרא rules on a destroyed palm: an Aramean palm is valued through its land, and a Persian palm follows the ריש גלותא. A new story about אליעזר זעירא begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: An animal ate budding grapes: two ways to value the loss
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא. If an animal ate סמדר, רבי יהושע values the grapes as if they were ripe. חכמים check how much the vineyard was worth before and after.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the animal ate budding grapes: רבי יהושע says we look at them as if they were grapes ready to be picked. חכמים say we look at how much the vineyard was worth before and how much it is worth now.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי is quoting a ברייתא that he will use as proof. It gives two opinions on how to value budding grapes that an animal ate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע treats the lost buds as if they were full, ripe grapes. חכמים instead compare the value of the vineyard before and after the damage. The wording of חכמים is the key point, because אביי will build his proof on it.

keyTerms.meaning: Grapes at the budding stage, just after the blossom
We look at it / we assess it (the court's appraisal)
Ready to be harvested (ripe grapes)
How much it was worth (before the damage)

steps.confusionAlert: This ברייתא is not a new topic. It is the source אביי brings to prove how to read the wording 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth' in the סוגיא just before this.

phrases.english: If the animal ate budding grapes
Rabbi Yehoshua says:
We view them as if they were
grapes ready to be picked
And the Rabbis say:
We see how much it was worth
phrases.notes: 'It' here means the vineyard, valued before the animal ate.

phrases.english: and how much it is worth now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues אביי's proof, which began just before this section.
steps.raayaObject: That the wording 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth' means appraisal relative to sixty.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about an animal eating סמדר, in the words of חכמים.

steps.title: רבי שמעון limits the Rabbis' rule to eaten branches
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן יהודה, quoting רבי שמעון, says the before-and-after appraisal applies only when the animal ate young vine shoots or fig shoots. If it ate the unripe fruit itself, we value it as ripe grapes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן יהודה says in the name of רבי שמעון: When does this apply? When the animal ate young vine branches or fig shoots. But if it ate unripe figs or unripe grapes, we view them as if they were grapes ready to be picked.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a third opinion. It narrows the rule of חכמים to a specific case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי שמעון, the field-based appraisal of חכמים is only for damage to branches and shoots. When actual young fruit is eaten, he agrees with רבי יהושע that it is valued as ripe fruit.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case was this said? (a phrase that limits a rule)
Young, tender branches of grapevines
Young shoots of fig trees
Unripe figs
Unripe grapes

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon:
In what case was this said?
When the animal ate young vine branches
or shoots of fig trees
but if it ate unripe figs or unripe grapes
we view them as if they were
grapes ready to be picked.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: בַּמֶּה דְּבָרִים אֲמוּרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limiting opinion to the same ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: Completes the text of the ברייתא that אביי is quoting.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The end of the סמדר ברייתא.

steps.title: The Rabbis don't say 'sixty' outright
steps.stepSummary: אביי points out that חכמים in this ברייתא only say 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth'. They never mention appraising against sixty.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, it teaches: 'And the חכמים say: we look at how much it was worth and how much it is worth.' And it does not say 'against sixty'!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי draws attention to the exact words of חכמים in the ברייתא. This sets up his next point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth' appears here with no mention of 'sixty'. This is the same wording that caused the question in the earlier ברייתא. אביי is preparing to show that this wording itself must mean 'sixty'.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, it teaches (a phrase that focuses on the part of a source that matters for the proof)
Against sixty: measuring the damaged part as part of a field sixty times bigger

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
And the Rabbis say:
We look at how much it was worth
and how much it is worth
and it does not say 'against sixty'!
phrases.notes: 'Sixty' is the משנה's rule: the damage is valued as part of an area sixty times bigger.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks out the key words from the ברייתא quoted in steps 1-2.
steps.raayaObject: The wording of חכמים, which leaves out 'sixty'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The words of חכמים in the סמדר ברייתא.

steps.title: It must mean sixty, so the other ברייתא means sixty too
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues that everyone must read חכמים here as meaning 'against sixty'. So the other ברייתא, which uses the same wording, also means 'against sixty'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what do you have to say? That it means against sixty. Here too, it means against sixty.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי finishes his proof. Since this wording must mean 'sixty', the same wording in the other ברייתא must mean 'sixty' too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier question was that a ברייתא said 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth' without saying 'sixty'. אביי shows that חכמים use the very same phrase, and it can only mean 'sixty'. So that short wording is simply a way of saying 'sixty', and the question falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, what must you say? (it forces the only possible reading)
Here too (applying the same reading to the case in question)

steps.whatToRemember: The phrase 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth' is a short way of saying the damage is appraised against sixty, as the משנה teaches.

phrases.english: Rather, what do you have to say?
That it means against sixty.
Here too, it means against sixty.
phrases.notes: 'Here' points back to the other ברייתא, the one the גמרא was asking about just before this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the point made in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the wording: the phrase 'how much it was worth and how much it is worth' is shown to mean 'sixty'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the ברייתא did not say 'sixty', we might have thought it means a simple before-and-after appraisal of the damaged part alone.
steps.terutzMaskana: The same wording in the חכמים's opinion must mean 'sixty', so the other ברייתא also means 'sixty'.

steps.title: אביי: two תנאים share the same view
steps.stepSummary: אביי states that רבי יוסי הגלילי and רבי ישמעאל hold the same opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: רבי יוסי הגלילי and רבי ישמעאל said the same thing.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי makes a new statement linking two תנאים. He says their two opinions are really one view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rulings that seemed separate are shown to rest on the same idea. Both hold that the appraisal is based on the produce that remains in the field, valued as it would grow and ripen.

keyTerms.meaning: They said the same thing: two scholars hold one view

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Yishmael
said the same thing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אָמְרוּ דָּבָר אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new statement by אביי after his proof is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוסי הגלילי and רבי ישמעאל share one opinion: the appraisal is based on the value of the produce once it ripens.

steps.title: The source for רבי יוסי הגלילי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the source for רבי יוסי הגלילי is the statement already quoted earlier.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי הגלילי: that is the statement we already said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins backing up what אביי said. It shows where רבי יוסי הגלילי holds this view, and it simply points back to his statement quoted earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי claimed that two תנאים agree that the damage is valued by what is left in the field, as it will grow and ripen. For the first one, רבי יוסי הגלילי, no new source is needed, because his view was already quoted earlier in the סוגיא.

keyTerms.meaning: This that we already said; it points back to an earlier quote.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: this that we said.
phrases.notes: The source is his statement quoted earlier on the daf, so the גמרא doesn't repeat it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first of the two sources for אביי's claim in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוסי הגלילי values the damage by what remains in the field as it ripens.
steps.raayaSupportSource: His statement quoted earlier in the sugya.

steps.title: The source for רבי ישמעאל: the best of the damaged person's field
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי ישמעאל reads 'מיטב' as the best of the damaged person's field. רבי עקיבא reads it as payment from the damager's best land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל: as a ברייתא teaches. 'The best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay' means the best of the damaged person's field and the best of the damaged person's vineyard. These are רבי ישמעאל's words. רבי עקיבא says: the verse only comes to let damaged people collect from the best-quality land, and by a קל וחומר the same applies to הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as the source for רבי ישמעאל. In it, he and רבי עקיבא argue over whose 'best' the פסוק means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי ישמעאל, 'מיטב' describes the field that was damaged, so it tells us how to measure the loss. For רבי עקיבא, 'מיטב' tells us what land the damager pays with: his own best land (עידית). The גמרא still has to explain how רבי ישמעאל's reading matches רבי יוסי הגלילי, and steps 8-10 do that.

keyTerms.meaning: The best part.
The person who was damaged.
Best-quality land.
An argument from a lighter case to a stricter one.
Property set aside for the בית המקדש.

steps.confusionAlert: Both תנאים use the same word 'מיטב', but in different ways. רבי ישמעאל means the damaged person's field. רבי עקיבא means the payer's land.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael: as it is taught:
'The best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay':
the best of the field of the damaged person,
and the best of the vineyard of the damaged person;
these are the words of Rabbi Yishmael.
Rabbi Akiva says:
the verse comes only
to let damaged people collect from the best-quality land,
phrases.notes: He means the damager's best land, not the damaged field.

phrases.english: and all the more so for consecrated property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second source for אביי's claim in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי ישמעאל, like רבי יוסי הגלילי, values the damage by what remains in the field as it grows.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on 'מיטב שדהו ומיטב כרמו ישלם'.

steps.title: Don't read רבי ישמעאל like רב אידי בר אבין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects reading רבי ישמעאל through רב אידי בר אבין's case, where the damager pays for the unknown bed as if it were the best one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't say that רבי ישמעאל means what רב אידי בר אבין said. רב אידי בר אבין said: for example, the animal ate one bed among the garden beds, and we don't know if that bed was poor or rich. The פסוק tells the owner: get up and pay for a rich bed, like the best one that is there now. We don't say that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks a different way of reading רבי ישמעאל's 'best of the damaged person's field'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אידי בר אבין reads 'מיטב' as a rule for cases of doubt. If we don't know which quality of bed was eaten, the owner pays as if it was the best bed still standing. If that were רבי ישמעאל's point, he would not match רבי יוסי הגלילי's view about valuing the growing produce. The גמרא rejects this reading, and step 9 gives the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: And don't say; it blocks a possible reading.
A garden bed.
Thin, poor quality.
Rich, good quality.

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא תֵּימָא כְּרַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין –
phrases.english: And do not say it is like Rav Idi bar Avin,
for Rav Idi bar Avin said:
for example, where it ate one bed among the garden beds,
and we don't know whether it was poor
or whether it was rich,
that the פסוק says: get up, pay for a rich one,
phrases.notes: The one speaking is the פסוק, telling the animal's owner what to pay.

phrases.english: like the best that is there now;
because this we do not say.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא תֵּימָא כְּרַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules out one way of reading the ברייתא from step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the reading of רבי ישמעאל through רב אידי בר אבין's case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That reading would charge the owner the top price when we are in doubt. Step 9 explains why that is wrong.

steps.title: Why not? The one who wants to collect must bring proof
steps.stepSummary: The reason for rejecting that reading: when we are in doubt, the person claiming money has to prove it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? The one who wants to take money from his friend has to bring the proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why we don't read רבי ישמעאל like רב אידי בר אבין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a case of doubt, the damaged person is the one trying to collect. Without proof that the eaten bed was a rich one, he only gets paid for a poor one. So רבי ישמעאל cannot mean 'pay the best price whenever we are unsure.'

keyTerms.meaning: The one who wants to take money from another must bring proof.
What is the reason?

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic rule of money law found all over ש״ס. Here it limits how far a פסוק can be read.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
The one who takes money from his fellow, the proof is on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? הַמּוֹצִיא מֵחֲבֵירוֹ עָלָיו הָרְאָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind the rejection in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי ישמעאל cannot mean what רב אידי בר אבין said.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The person collecting has to bring proof, so we cannot charge the top price when we are unsure.

steps.title: 'מיטב' means the best the field was going to become
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל's 'מיטב' means the best that lies ahead for the field: the way the crop would have grown.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means the best that is ahead of it. And what is that? The way it grows up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the right reading of רבי ישמעאל. The 'best' of the damaged field is what the crop was going to grow into.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We appraise the damaged field by what remains in it and how it was going to grow, not by guessing at the best bed. This is exactly רבי יוסי הגלילי's view, so אביי's claim from step 5 holds up.

keyTerms.meaning: That is ahead of it, still to come.
The way it grows up.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוסי הגלילי and רבי ישמעאל agree that the damage is valued by what remains in the field as it grows. For רבי ישמעאל, 'מיטב של ניזק' means the field as it was going to grow. It does not mean paying the top price in a case of doubt, because the one who wants to collect must bring proof.

phrases.english: Rather, with the best that is ahead of it,
and what is it? The way it grows up.
phrases.notes: He means the value the crop would have reached as it kept growing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reading from step 8 with the correct one.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי ישמעאל's 'מיטב' looks at how the remaining crop was going to grow, which is the same as רבי יוסי הגלילי's view.

steps.title: Quoting רבי שמעון בן יהודה and drawing an inference about budding grapes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא: the normal appraisal applies only when the animal ate young vine branches or fig shoots. It infers that for budding grapes we value them as if they were ripe grapes ready to be picked.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: רבי שמעון בן יהודה says in the name of רבי שמעון: When does this rule apply? When the animal ate young vine branches and fig shoots. This implies that if it ate budding grapes, we view them as if they were grapes ready to be picked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the ברייתא and draws a conclusion about budding grapes (סמדר). This is setting up the next move, where the גמרא will show a problem with that conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא limits the normal appraisal to vine branches and fig shoots. So anything else, like budding grapes, must get the better treatment: we value them as if they were full grapes ready to be picked.

keyTerms.meaning: 'In what case are these words said?', a way of limiting a rule to certain cases
Young, tender branches of grapevines
Young shoots of fig trees
Budding grapes, at the very first stage after the blossom
Grapes ready to be picked, meaning fully ripe

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: This goes back to the ברייתא quoted earlier, to look at it more closely.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon:
In what case is this said?
When the animal ate young branches of vines
and shoots of fig trees.
This implies: budding grapes
we view them as if they were
grapes ready to be picked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the meaning of 'מיטב' to looking closely at the words of the ברייתא about the eaten vineyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The normal appraisal is limited to vine branches and fig shoots. By inference, budding grapes are valued as if they were ripe grapes.

steps.title: The end of the ברייתא implies the opposite about budding grapes
steps.stepSummary: The end of the ברייתא gives the 'ready to be picked' value only for unripe figs or half-ripe grapes. That implies budding grapes get only the ordinary before-and-after appraisal, which contradicts the first part.
steps.simpleTranslation: But look at the end: if it ate unripe figs or half-ripe grapes, that is when we view them as grapes ready to be picked. This implies that for budding grapes we only check how much the field is worth now and how much it was worth before!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the inference from the first part by pointing to the end of the same ברייתא, which seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part implies budding grapes get the generous 'ripe grapes' value. The end gives that value only to unripe figs and half-ripe grapes, so budding grapes would get just the plain loss in value. The same ברייתא cannot say both.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Say the latter clause', used to show that the end of a source contradicts its beginning
Unripe figs
Half-ripe grapes, past the budding stage but not yet ripe

keyTerms.term: כַּמָּה הִיא יָפָה וְכַמָּה הָיְתָה יָפָה
keyTerms.meaning: How much it is worth now and how much it was worth before, meaning the ordinary appraisal of the loss

steps.confusionAlert: Budding grapes (סמדר) come before half-ripe grapes (בוסר). The question is whether the earliest stage also gets the 'ready to be picked' value.

phrases.english: Say the latter clause:
If it ate unripe figs or half-ripe grapes,
that is where we view them as if they were
grapes ready to be picked.
This implies: budding grapes
we view how much it is worth now
and how much it was worth before!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference drawn in step 11 by using the end of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that budding grapes are valued as ripe grapes.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Inside one source, the beginning and the end imply opposite rules for סמדר.

steps.title: רבינא reads the ברייתא as one connected statement
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says to join the two parts. The ordinary appraisal is only for vine branches and fig shoots. Budding grapes, unripe figs and half-ripe grapes are all valued as ripe grapes ready to be picked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Join them and teach it like this: When does this rule apply? When it ate young vine branches and fig shoots. But if it ate budding grapes, unripe figs or half-ripe grapes, we view them as grapes ready to be picked.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא solves the contradiction by reading the two parts of the ברייתא as one sentence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The end is not a separate rule that leaves out budding grapes. It explains the first part, and סמדר is added to the list. So budding grapes get the 'ready to be picked' value, just as the first part implied.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Bind and teach', meaning read two parts of a source together as one statement

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבינא, in the view of רבי שמעון בן יהודה, only branches and shoots get the plain appraisal. Budding grapes, unripe figs and half-ripe grapes are valued as ripe grapes.

phrases.english: Ravina said: Bind them together and teach:
phrases.notes: He means: don't read the beginning and the end as two separate rules. Read them as one sentence.

phrases.english: In what case is this said?
When the animal ate young branches of vines
and shoots of fig trees.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אָכְלָה סְמָדַר פַּגִּין אוֹ בוֹסֶר –
phrases.english: But if it ate budding grapes, unripe figs, or half-ripe grapes,
we view them as if they were
grapes ready to be picked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source: the two parts are joined into one statement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The end of the ברייתא was a separate rule implying that budding grapes get only the ordinary appraisal.
steps.terutzMaskana: The end belongs with the beginning. Budding grapes, unripe figs and half-ripe grapes all get the ripe-grapes value.

steps.title: Then רבי שמעון בן יהודה says the same as רבי יהושע
steps.stepSummary: If budding grapes are valued as ripe grapes, then רבי שמעון בן יהודה says exactly what רבי יהושע said. So why list them as two separate opinions?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, רבי שמעון בן יהודה is the same as רבי יהושע!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא's reading: it makes רבי שמעון בן יהודה's opinion identical to רבי יהושע's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע already said that budding grapes are viewed as grapes ready to be picked. If רבי שמעון בן יהודה says the same, there is no reason to quote him as a separate opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If so', which introduces a problem that follows from the answer just given
'That is the same as', used to say two opinions are identical

phrases.english: If so,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה הַיְינוּ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ!
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda is the same as Rabbi Yehoshua!
phrases.notes: רבי יהושע already said budding grapes are viewed as grapes ready to be picked.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה הַיְינוּ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks a result of רבינא's answer in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's joined reading of רבי שמעון בן יהודה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two opinions are not quoted separately unless they are different. Under רבינא's reading, these two are the same.

steps.title: They differ about the weakening of the vine, but we don't know who holds what
steps.stepSummary: The difference between them is the 'weakening of the vine': whether we subtract the benefit the vine got from no longer having to feed the grapes. The גמרא does not say which one holds which side.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them: the weakening of the vine. But we do not know which one holds which view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two opinions are not the same. They argue about one detail of the appraisal, though the גמרא admits it cannot say who holds which side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Growing grapes draw strength from the vine. Once the animal ate them, the vine is spared that drain. One opinion subtracts this benefit from the payment, and the other does not. So the opinions differ, even though both use the 'ready to be picked' value.

keyTerms.meaning: 'There is a difference between them', which points to a practical difference between two opinions
The weakening of the vine caused by the grapes growing on it
'But they are not identified': we know there is an argument but not which side each one holds

steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions value budding grapes as ripe grapes. They differ only on whether to subtract the benefit to the vine. The next step, where אביי speaks, shows who holds which view.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them:
the weakening of the vine.
phrases.notes: Growing grapes drain the vine's strength, so eating them spares the vine. Do we take that benefit off the payment?

phrases.english: But it is not defined which one holds which view.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to a practical difference between the two opinions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two opinions were exactly the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: They argue about subtracting the benefit to the vine, though we don't know which one holds which view.

steps.title: אביי: We can tell who holds which side
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the two opinions can be identified: רבי שמעון בן יהודה is the תנא who takes the vine's weakening into account.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The opinions can clearly be identified! Who is the תנא who takes the weakening of the vine into account? It is רבי שמעון בן יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the open question from the last step by naming רבי שמעון בן יהודה as the one who considers the vine's weakening. He brings his proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 left it unclear which תנא subtracts the vine's benefit, meaning the vine no longer has to feed the grapes. אביי says it is רבי שמעון בן יהודה. So the damager gets credit for that benefit. By elimination, רבי יהושע does not subtract it.

keyTerms.meaning: They are defined, clearly identifiable
Weakening of the vine, the strain that growing grapes puts on the vine
A sage of the משנה period

phrases.english: Abaye said: They are clearly identifiable!
phrases.notes: Literally 'they are defined and defined.' He means we can tell which תנא holds which side.

phrases.english: Who is the tanna who takes the weakening of the vine into account?
It is Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills in what step 15 left open: which תנא holds which side of the vine-weakening question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying the positions: the dispute is assigned to specific תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought there is no way to know who holds which side.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי שמעון בן יהודה subtracts the vine-weakening benefit. רבי יהושע does not.

steps.title: Proof from the rapist who does not pay for pain
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי שמעון בן יהודה exempts a rapist from paying for pain, because the woman would have felt that pain anyway with her husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי שמעון בן יהודה says in the name of רבי שמעון בן מנסיא: A rapist does not pay for the pain, because she will eventually suffer that pain with her husband. They said to him: A woman who has relations willingly is not comparable to a woman who has relations by force.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings a ברייתא to prove that רבי שמעון בן יהודה takes into account a loss that would have happened anyway. This explains why he also considers the vine's weakening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן יהודה reasons that the pain was going to come anyway, so the damager does not pay for it. In the same way, the vine would have been weakened by the grapes anyway, so the damager gets credit for saving it from that. The חכמים disagree here, but אביי only needs the opinion of רבי שמעון בן יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: A rapist, who must pay the victim several payments
Pain, one of the payments for damage
Willingly

steps.confusionAlert: The חכמים reject this reasoning in the ברייתא, but that does not weaken אביי's proof. He only needs to show how רבי שמעון בן יהודה thinks.

phrases.english: as it was taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says
in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya:
A rapist does not pay for the pain,
because she will eventually suffer that pain with her husband.
phrases.notes: He means the pain of a first time together, which she would feel anyway once she marries.

phrases.english: They said to him:
A woman who has relations willingly is not comparable
to a woman who has relations by force.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן מְנַסְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind אביי's claim in step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי שמעון בן יהודה is the one who takes the vine's weakening into account
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא where רבי שמעון בן יהודה exempts a rapist from paying for pain that would have come anyway

steps.title: אביי: Other תנאים say the same thing
steps.stepSummary: אביי says that certain other תנאים agree with the idea of רבי שמעון בן יהודה. He then asks which case those תנאים were talking about.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: These תנאים and רבי שמעון בן יהודה said the same thing. רבי שמעון בן יהודה: what we just said. These תנאים, what is their case?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי points out that other תנאים share the same idea. He ends with a question that sets up the next step, where their ברייתא is quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shared idea is that when the damage also saves the owner something, that saving is subtracted from the payment. For רבי שמעון בן יהודה we already saw the source. The case of the other תנאים still needs to be shown.

keyTerms.meaning: The same thing, one shared idea
What we just said
These תנאים, the ones about to be quoted
What is it? A request for the source

phrases.english: Abaye said: These tanna'im,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה, אָמְרוּ דָּבָר אֶחָד.
phrases.english: and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, said the same thing.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה – הָא דַּאֲמַרַן.
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda: what we just said.
These tanna'im, what is their case?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הָנֵי תַּנָּאֵי, וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוּדָה, אָמְרוּ דָּבָר אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the idea of רבי שמעון בן יהודה from step 17 to other תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Other תנאים share the view of רבי שמעון בן יהודה that the owner's savings are subtracted from the damages.

steps.title: רבי יוסי and בן עזאי: Subtract the savings from a miscarriage
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי יוסי says to subtract the midwife cost. בן עזאי says to subtract the cost of extra food.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי יוסי says: Minus the midwife. בן עזאי says: Minus the food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers אביי's question by quoting a ברייתא about paying for the babies lost when someone causes a miscarriage. Both תנאים subtract something the husband saves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because she miscarried, the husband no longer has to pay for a midwife, and no longer has to provide the extra food a pregnant woman needs. רבי יוסי subtracts the midwife cost and בן עזאי subtracts the food. Both, like רבי שמעון בן יהודה, credit the damager with what the owner saved.

keyTerms.meaning: Minus, deduct
A midwife
Food, here the extra food a pregnant woman needs

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:
phrases.notes: The case is someone who hits a pregnant woman and she miscarries, so he must pay for the babies (שמות 21:22).

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: Minus the cost of a midwife.
Ben Azzai says: Minus the cost of food.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: נְכֵי חַיָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question at the end of step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case the other תנאים were discussing
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Paying for a miscarriage: רבי יוסי subtracts the midwife cost, and בן עזאי subtracts the extra food.

steps.title: Why the midwife view surely includes food, but not the reverse
steps.stepSummary: Whoever subtracts the midwife surely subtracts the food. בן עזאי subtracts only the food, because the husband can say his wife does not need a midwife.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says 'minus the midwife' surely also says 'minus the food.' But the one who says 'minus the food' does not subtract the midwife, because the husband can tell him: My wife is capable and does not need a midwife.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the two opinions in the ברייתא relate to each other. It shows that רבי יוסי subtracts more than בן עזאי does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every pregnant woman needs extra food, so that saving is certain. Not every woman needs a midwife, so that saving is less certain. Therefore רבי יוסי, who subtracts even the uncertain midwife cost, surely subtracts the food. בן עזאי stops at the food, because the husband can claim he never would have paid for a midwife.

keyTerms.meaning: All the more so
Capable, skilled
Does not need

steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון בן יהודה, רבי יוסי and בן עזאי all share one idea: when the damage also saves the owner an expense or a loss, that saving comes off the payment. That is why רבי שמעון בן יהודה subtracts the vine's weakening.

phrases.english: The one who says 'minus the midwife,'
all the more so says 'minus the food.'
But the one who says 'minus the food,'
does not subtract the midwife,
because the husband can say to the damager:
My wife is capable,
and does not need a midwife.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר נְכֵי חַיָּה, כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן נְכֵי מְזוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the two opinions in the ברייתא of step 19 relate to each other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The midwife saving is less certain than the food saving, so רבי יוסי subtracts more than בן עזאי does.

steps.title: רב פפא and רב הונא ruled like רב נחמן: appraise in sixty
steps.stepSummary: A report of an actual court case: רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע followed רב נחמן and valued the palm בששים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא and רב הונא, son of רב יהושע, decided an actual case like רב נחמן: they valued the tree in sixty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the question of how to value a destroyed date palm. It reports that two אמוראים decided a real case following רב נחמן's method of 'sixty'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'בששים' is רב נחמן's method from the earlier discussion. The tree is not priced alone. Its loss is measured against a much larger field. The words 'עבוד עובדא' tell us this was a real ruling in court, not just theory, so it carries extra weight.

keyTerms.meaning: They did an actual deed, meaning they ruled in a real case
Like him, following his opinion
In sixty: valuing the damage against an area sixty times larger

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
phrases.english: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
acted in a real case following Rav Nachman
in sixty.
phrases.notes: This points back to רב נחמן's earlier method: value the tree as part of a field sixty times bigger.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion (vine, pain, midwife) and returns to the main topic of valuing a damaged date palm.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע valued a destroyed palm בששים, like רב נחמן.

steps.title: Another version: they appraised the palm by its patch of land
steps.stepSummary: A different report says the same two אמוראים valued the palm by how much it added to the small plot of land it stood on.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: רב פפא and רב הונא, son of רב יהושע, valued the palm together with the small patch of land it stood on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of what רב פפא and רב הונא actually did. In this version they did not use 'sixty'. They valued the tree through its own small plot of land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the court asks how much the small patch was worth with the tree and how much it is worth without it. The difference is what the damager pays. This is a different measuring method from 'sixty', so the two versions disagree about what these אמוראים held.

keyTerms.meaning: Another version of the report
They appraised, they set a value
Date palm
A small patch of land

steps.confusionAlert: Do not combine the two versions. The first says they used 'sixty'. The second says they used the small patch of land. They are two competing reports of the same ruling.

phrases.english: Another version:

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
phrases.english: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
appraised the palm along with a small patch of land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a competing report of the same ruling from step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to this version, the palm is valued by the change in worth of its own small patch of land.

steps.title: Final ruling: Aramean palm by the land, Persian palm like the ריש גלותא
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה depends on the type of palm. A cheap Aramean palm follows רב פפא and רב הונא. A valuable Persian palm follows the ריש גלותא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה follows רב פפא and רב הונא, son of רב יהושע, for an Aramean palm. The הלכה follows the ריש גלותא for a Persian palm.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final practical ruling. It does not pick one method for every tree. It splits the ruling by the kind of palm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An Aramean palm is lower quality, so it is valued through the land, like רב פפא and רב הונא. A Persian palm is high quality, and each tree is valuable on its own. So it follows the ריש גלותא, who valued the tree itself rather than measuring it through the land.

keyTerms.meaning: And the practical ruling is
The Exilarch, leader of the Jews in Babylonia
Aramean date palm, a cheaper kind
Persian date palm, a valuable kind

steps.whatToRemember: How you value a destroyed palm depends on the tree. A cheap Aramean palm is valued through its land. A valuable Persian palm is valued on its own, like the ריש גלותא said.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the method of appraisal follows real market value. Since a Persian palm is valuable by itself, measuring it only through the land would underpay the owner.

phrases.english: And the halacha follows Rav Pappa
and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
for an Aramean palm,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the letters in round brackets and some leave them out. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: and the halacha follows the Exilarch
for a Persian palm.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the practical הלכה after the two reports, splitting the ruling by type of palm.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An Aramean palm is valued through its patch of land. A Persian palm is valued on its own, following the ריש גלותא.

steps.title: A new story begins about אליעזר זעירא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new story by naming its main character, אליעזר זעירא.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליעזר זעירא...
steps.whatsHappening: This line only introduces the next story by naming the person it is about. The story itself continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing has been said yet. The name is the setup. The details of what happened to אליעזר זעירא come right after this line.

phrases.english: Eliezer Ze'eira

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the final ruling on palms, the גמרא begins a new story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup line only: it introduces the story of אליעזר זעירא.
